p: Timothy's name stands beside Paul's, as in 2 Corinthians, Philippians, the Thessalonian letters and Philemon.
b: Timothy, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father from Lystra (Acts 16:1), is named as a co-sender, as in 2 Corinthians 1:1, Philippians 1:1 and Philemon 1. The letter then speaks in Paul's voice ('I, Paul', 1:23; 4:18). Eduard Schweizer suggested that Paul and Timothy wrote it together, and James Dunn's commentary is cited for the possibility that Timothy was the secretary who wrote it down. See the authorship section of the opening pages.

p: Hagioi means 'holy ones': people set apart for God, not a special class of believers.
b: The Greek tois en Kolossais hagiois kai pistois adelphois can be read two ways: 'to the saints and faithful brothers' (two nouns) or 'to the holy and faithful brothers' (two adjectives for one group). The Plain English Translation keeps 'saints' as a noun, as in Paul's other greetings (Romans 1:7; Ephesians 1:1), and lets 'the faithful brothers in Christ' describe them. Either way, 'saints' is Paul's word for all the believers in a place, as in the Old Testament's 'holy people' (Exodus 19:6), not a title for a few outstanding Christians.
orig: ἁγίοις (hagiois), 'holy ones'

t: "Brothers" and the women of the church
p: The plural adelphoi takes in the whole family of believers, women as well as men.
b: Paul writes adelphoi, 'brothers'. In Greek the masculine plural is the normal word for a mixed group, as when a family's sons and daughters are called 'brothers'. This site keeps 'brothers' in the Plain English Translation, as Acts and Romans do, with the gloss 'brothers and sisters'. In Colossians the point is not abstract: a church meets in Nympha's house (4:15), and the household code speaks to wives as members who hear the letter (3:18).
orig: ἀδελφοῖς (adelphois)

p: A small town in Phrygia, about 12 miles (19 km) east of Laodicea, overshadowed by its richer neighbors.
b: Colossae stood on the Lycus River in Phrygia, in the Roman province of Asia, near Laodicea and Hierapolis (2:1; 4:13). Strabo says the district around Laodicea made great money from the fine wool of its sheep, and that the Colossians did so from a color of wool named after their town (Geography 12.8.16, quoted by Lightfoot). By Paul's time it had been outgrown by Laodicea. J. B. Lightfoot wrote in 1875 that 'Colossae was the least important Church' to which Paul sent a letter. Its mound, near modern Honaz in Turkey, was surveyed by Pamukkale University from 2021, and excavation began in 2025. That year the team reported about 60 rock-cut tombs in one burial ground, with amulets and charms among the finds.

a: Every time we pray for you
p: Paul's letters open with thanks to God for the readers, the normal shape of a Greek letter turned into prayer.
b: Ancient letters often began with a prayer to the gods for the reader's health. Paul turns this into thanks for what God has done among the readers (Romans 1:8; 1 Corinthians 1:4; Philippians 1:3). The Greek word pantote, 'always', can go with 'we thank' or with 'praying'; the Plain English Translation lets 'every time we pray' carry it. Thanks runs through the whole letter (1:12; 2:7; 3:15-17; 4:2), more than in any other short letter of Paul's.

a: the hope that is set aside for you in the heavens
p: Paul's three, faith, love and hope, appear together, and hope is the root of the other two.
b: The readers have faith and love (1:4) 'because of the hope'. Faith, love and hope are the three Paul names in 1 Corinthians 13:13 and 1 Thessalonians 1:3. Here the hope is not a feeling but something 'set aside' (apokeimenēn, stored away, as a prize is kept for the winner, 2 Timothy 4:8) in the heavens. This prepares for 3:1-4, where the believers' life itself is 'kept hidden away with Christ in God'.
orig: τὴν ἐλπίδα τὴν ἀποκειμένην (tēn elpida tēn apokeimenēn)

a: All over the world it keeps bearing fruit and growing
p: The words of Genesis 1:28, 'be fruitful and multiply', may lie behind the pair.
b: The pair 'bearing fruit and growing' comes again in 1:10. The pair may echo the creation blessing of Genesis 1:28 (in the Septuagint, auxanesthe kai plēthynesthe, 'grow and multiply'), now said of the good news, as Acts says that 'the word of God kept growing' (Acts 6:7; Acts 12:24). The claim 'all over the world' is a claim about the reach of the message across the Roman world, the same kind of language as 1:23 and Romans 1:8.

p: A Colossian believer who brought the good news to the Lycus valley and later reported to Paul.
b: Epaphras was 'one of your own' (4:12) and worked hard for the churches of Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis (4:13). This verse implies that he, not Paul, first taught the Colossians, which fits 2:1: they had never seen Paul's face. Acts 19:10 says that during Paul's two years in Ephesus 'everyone living in Asia heard the Lord's word', and Epaphras may have been one of the ways that happened. Philemon 23 calls him Paul's 'fellow captive'. His name is a short form of Epaphroditus, but most scholars do not identify him with the Epaphroditus of Philippi (Philippians 2:25).

p: Syndoulos puts Epaphras beside Paul as one more slave of the same Master.
b: Syndoulos is 'fellow slave'. Paul calls himself and his coworkers slaves of Christ (Romans 1:1; Philippians 1:1), and Epaphras is called 'a slave of Christ' in 4:12. Many English Bibles soften doulos to 'servant'; this site keeps 'slave', because in a city where many people were slaves, the word said plainly that a believer belongs to a Master. Tychicus is also a 'fellow slave' (4:7). The word is kept apart from diakonos, 'servant', later in this verse.
orig: συνδούλου (syndoulou)

a: the full knowledge of what he wants
p: Epignosis and sophia are words the letter takes back from those who claimed special knowledge.
b: Paul piles up words for knowing: epignōsis ('full knowledge', 1:9, 10; 2:2; 3:10), sophia ('wisdom', 1:9, 28; 2:3, 23; 3:16; 4:5) and synesis ('understanding', 1:9; 2:2). Read with chapter 2, these look chosen on purpose: the teachers at Colossae offered wisdom and visions (2:8, 18, 23), and Paul answers that every treasure of wisdom and knowledge is hidden in Christ (2:3). 'What he wants' translates to thelēma autou, 'his will'.
orig: τὴν ἐπίγνωσιν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ (tēn epignōsin tou thelēmatos autou)

p: Paul's word for daily conduct is the Hebrew picture of life as a road walked.
b: Peripateō, 'walk', is the Jewish way of speaking about how one lives, from the Hebrew halakh; Jewish law is still called halakhah, 'the walking'. The letter uses it at its turning points: walk worthy of the Lord (1:10), walk in him (2:6), you once walked in these things (3:7), walk in wisdom toward outsiders (4:5). The Plain English Translation keeps 'walk' so that the reader can follow the thread.
orig: περιπατῆσαι (peripatēsai)

a: the lot of the saints in the light
t: The lot, as in the land of Canaan
p: Kleros is the 'lot' by which Joshua shared out the land; Gentiles now share Israel's inheritance.
b: Tēn merida tou klērou is literally 'the share of the lot'. In the Septuagint, klēros ('lot') and meris ('share') are the words for the tribes' portions of Canaan, given out by lot (Joshua 19:9). Paul uses the language of Israel's inheritance for Gentile believers. 'In the light' sets the inheritance in God's realm, against 'the authority of darkness' in the next verse.

t: Out of darkness, into a kingdom
p: A picture of a population moved from one ruler's land to another's.
b: Exousia tou skotous is 'the authority of darkness', the same phrase Jesus uses at his arrest in Luke 22:53. The verb methistēmi, 'moved', was used for moving whole peoples from one land to another, as kings of the ancient world did. Believers are pictured as transferred out from under one ruler and into the kingdom of another. The language of rescue from darkness to light also matches Paul's commission in Acts 26:18.
orig: ἐκ τῆς ἐξουσίας τοῦ σκότους (ek tēs exousias tou skotous)

p: A Hebrew-style phrase for 'his dearly loved Son'.
b: Paul writes tou huiou tēs agapēs autou, literally 'the Son of his love'. This is a Semitic way of saying 'his beloved Son', like 'son of peace' for a peaceful person. The Plain English Translation keeps the literal form because it may say more than 'beloved': the Son is the one in whom the Father's love is found. Compare the voice at Jesus' baptism, 'You are my dearly loved Son' (Mark 1:11), and 'the Beloved' in Ephesians 1:6.
orig: τοῦ υἱοῦ τῆς ἀγάπης αὐτοῦ (tou huiou tēs agapēs autou)

t: Redemption, and the parallel in Ephesians
p: Colossians 1:14 and Ephesians 1:7 open with the same words; Ephesians adds 'by his blood'.
b: 'In him we have redemption by his blood' (Ephesians 1:7). Colossians has the same opening Greek without 'by his blood', and says 'sins' (hamartiōn) where Ephesians says 'trespasses'. The Plain English Translation follows Ephesians' wording exactly where the Greek is the same. Apolytrōsis is 'being set free by a price paid', the word used for buying back a slave or a captive. Here it is defined as the forgiveness of sins, so the stress falls on release rather than on a price.
orig: τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν (tēn apolytrōsin)

a: He is the image of the God who cannot be seen
t: The image of the invisible God
p: Eikon echoes Genesis 1:27 and Jewish writing about Wisdom as God's image.
b: Eikōn is the word of Genesis 1:26-27 in the Septuagint, 'in God's image he created him'. Paul says Christ is 'the image of God' in 2 Corinthians 4:4, and the new self is renewed 'to match the image' of its creator in 3:10. Jewish writers used the same word for Wisdom: Wisdom of Solomon 7:26 calls her 'an image of his goodness' (eikōn tēs agathotētos autou). In the ancient world an image made someone present who could not be seen directly. The point is that the unseen God is seen in Christ (compare John 1:18).
orig: εἰκὼν τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ἀοράτου (eikōn tou theou tou aoratou)
r: Genesis 1:27; 2 Corinthians 4:4; John 1:18; 3:10; Wisdom of Solomon 7:26

t: Firstborn: first in time, or first in rank?
p: Prototokos can mean the first one born, or the heir who holds first place. It shaped the creeds.
b: Prōtotokos pasēs ktiseōs is 'firstborn of all creation'. The genitive 'of' can mean 'first of the creatures' or 'firstborn over creation'. In the Old Testament 'firstborn' is often a rank: 'Israel is my son, my firstborn' (Exodus 4:22), and of David's heir, 'I, for my part, will make him firstborn' (Psalm 89:27). The next verse gives the reason, 'because in him all things were created', which places him on the Creator's side. Arius in the 300s read the word as 'first created'; Athanasius answered that 'firstborn of creation' is said 'because of brethren' and that the Son is 'other than the whole creation' (Orations against the Arians 2.62-64). The New World Translation of Jehovah's Witnesses reads it as 'the first creation by Jehovah God'. See the card below.
orig: πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως (prōtotokos pasēs ktiseōs)

a: in him all things were created
t: In him, through him, for him
p: Three little words, 'in', 'through' and 'for', say how Christ stands toward everything that exists.
b: The verse is framed by 'in him' (en autō) and 'through him and for him' (di' autou kai eis auton). 'In him' may mean 'in his sphere' or 'by means of him'; 'through him' makes him the agent, as in 1 Corinthians 8:6, 'All things are through him, and we are through him', and John 1:3; 'for him' (eis auton) makes him the goal, a thing Paul elsewhere says of God (Romans 11:36). The tense changes from 'were created' (a past act) to 'have been created' (a lasting state).
orig: ἐν αὐτῷ ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα (en autō ektisthē ta panta)

a: thrones or lordships or rulers or authorities
p: Four ranks of unseen powers, all made in Christ, including those the Colossians may have feared.
b: Jewish writings of the time divided the angels into ranks. Paul's point is that whatever the ranks, they are creatures made in Christ. The same 'rulers and authorities' are under Christ as head (2:10) and stripped at the cross (2:15). The list fits a church tempted toward 'the worship of angels' (2:18). This site renders the four words the same way in Ephesians 1:21 ('ruler, authority, power and lordship').
orig: θρόνοι, κυριότητες, ἀρχαί, ἐξουσίαι (thronoi, kyriotētes, archai, exousiai)

a: all things hold together in him
p: Synesteken is the word Greek thinkers used for what keeps the world from falling apart.
b: Synestēken, a perfect of synistēmi, means 'stand together, cohere'. Greek philosophers asked what holds the universe together, and the Stoics answered with the divine reason (Logos) that runs through all things. Jewish writers said something like it of God's word: in the Greek of Sirach 43:26, 'by his word all things are put together' (synkeitai). Colossians says it of Christ.
orig: τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκεν (ta panta en autō synestēken)

a: the head of the body, the church
p: Christ is the head and the church his body; in Ephesians the same picture is pressed further.
b: In 1 Corinthians 12 and Romans 12 the church is a body whose parts need one another, and the head is one part among them (1 Corinthians 12:21). In Colossians and Ephesians Christ is the head and the church is his body (2:19; Ephesians 1:22-23; 4:15-16). 'The church' may be an added gloss in a hymn that first said 'head of the body', meaning the cosmos, as Greek writers called the universe a body with a divine head; many critical scholars think so. The letter as it stands applies the picture to the church.
orig: ἡ κεφαλὴ τοῦ σώματος τῆς ἐκκλησίας (hē kephalē tou sōmatos tēs ekklēsias)

p: The second half of the hymn starts again from 'firstborn', now of the new creation.
b: The hymn has two halves that mirror each other: 'firstborn of all creation' (1:15) and 'firstborn from the dead' (1:18), with 'in him ... through him ... for him' in each. The resurrection is the beginning of a new creation. Revelation 1:5 calls Jesus 'the firstborn of the dead', and 1 Corinthians 15:20 calls him 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep'. 'The beginning' (archē) may echo Genesis 1:1 and Proverbs 8:22.

a: all the fullness was pleased to make its home
p: The Greek does not name a subject for 'was pleased': either 'all the fullness' or God.
b: Literally, 'in him was pleased all the fullness to dwell'. Either 'all the fullness' is the subject (the Plain English Translation), or the subject is God, unnamed ('God was pleased to have all the fullness dwell in him'). Since 'to reconcile ... to himself' follows, many take God as the one acting, and 'the fullness' as God in his fullness, as 2:9 spells out: 'the fullness of deity'. Plērōma later became a technical word for the world of divine beings in second-century Gnostic systems; Colossians uses it without that system and locates all of it in Christ.
orig: πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα κατοικῆσαι (pan to plērōma katoikēsai)

a: to reconcile all things to himself
t: Reconciling all things: does everyone end up saved?
p: The hymn says all things in earth and heaven are reconciled. Readers differ on what that includes.
b: Paul elsewhere says 'God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself' (2 Corinthians 5:19). Here the reach is wider still, 'all things ... on the earth or ... in the heavens'. Some Christians from Origen onward have read this as hope that every creature will finally be restored (apokatastasis); modern universalists cite it with 1 Corinthians 15:28 and Romans 5:18. Most interpreters read 'reconcile' here as 'bring back under Christ's peace': the hostile powers are made to submit (2:15), not saved, and the next verses tie the readers' share in it to continuing in the faith (1:23).

a: making peace through the blood of his cross
t: Peace by the blood of the cross
p: Ephesians 2:13-16 says the same of Jew and Gentile; here it is said of the whole universe.
b: 'The blood of Christ did it' (Ephesians 2:13), and Christ came 'making peace' between Jew and Gentile and reconciled 'both to God in one body through the cross' (Ephesians 2:15-16). The Plain English Translation uses Ephesians' wording where the Greek matches. In Colossians the peace reaches the whole created order, and only in 1:21-22 is it applied to the readers. Peace (eirēnē) for a Jewish reader is shalom, wholeness and right relationship, not only the end of war.

a: in the body of his flesh
p: A blunt phrase: reconciliation happened in a real human body that died.
b: 'The body of his flesh' sounds doubled in English. It insists that the one in whom 'all the fullness' lives (1:19) reconciled people in an ordinary body of flesh and blood, through death. If the teachers at Colossae despised the body (2:23) or looked for a fullness above the physical world, this phrase answers them. The same Greek words come back in 2:11, for what is stripped off in 'the circumcision of Christ'.
orig: ἐν τῷ σώματι τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ (en tō sōmati tēs sarkos autou)

t: Holy and without blame, as in Ephesians
p: The same words as Ephesians 1:4, with a courtroom word added: 'free of any charge'.
b: Ephesians 1:4 has 'to be holy and without blame before him in love', and the Plain English Translation uses the same words for the same Greek. Amōmos, 'without blame', is the Septuagint word for an animal with no defect, fit to be offered (Leviticus 22:21). Colossians adds anenklētos, 'free of any charge', a legal word: no one can bring a case. The picture moves from the altar to the court.
orig: ἁγίους καὶ ἀμώμους καὶ ἀνεγκλήτους (hagious kai amōmous kai anenklētous)

a: if you stay in the faith
t: "If": a condition or a confident hope?
p: The 'if' joins the readers' future to their staying in the faith. Traditions weigh it differently.
b: Ei ge is 'if indeed' and can lean toward 'since' ('if, as I am sure, you stay'). Those who teach that true believers cannot finally fall away (Reformed, many Baptists) read the 'if' as the means God uses to keep his people, or as a test showing who is real. Those who teach that believers can fall away (Catholic, Orthodox, Wesleyan) read it as a real condition. The building words ('foundation laid', 'standing firm') prepare for 2:7.
orig: εἴ γε ἐπιμένετε τῇ πίστει (ei ge epimenete tē pistei)

p: An overstatement in the style of the Old Testament, meaning the message has gone far and wide.
b: En pasē ktisei tē hypo ton ouranon can be 'in all creation under heaven' or 'to every creature under heaven'. Paul knew that much of the world had not yet heard (Romans 15:20-24). The phrase claims that the good news is meant for every creature and has already spread across the known world, as 1:6 says. It may also answer a teaching that kept full knowledge for a few.
orig: ἐν πάσῃ κτίσει (en pasē ktisei)

a: What is still missing from Christ's hardships
t: Filling up what Christ's sufferings lack
p: Does Paul add to Christ's saving work? Almost no one says so. The question is what else he means.
b: Antanaplērō ta hysterēmata tōn thlipseōn tou Christou: 'I fill up in turn what is lacking of the afflictions of Christ'. Paul never calls Christ's death a thlipsis; the word means troubles and hardships. Readings: (1) Christ suffers in his body, the church, and his members' sufferings are his (compare Acts 9:4, 'why are you persecuting me?'); (2) Jewish hope expected a fixed measure of 'messianic woes' before the end, and Paul takes up a share so that others suffer less; (3) Paul's own sufferings complete what his apostolic work requires. Catholic teaching draws from it the value of suffering joined to Christ (Salvifici Doloris 24); Calvin rejected its use for a treasury of merits. See the card below.
orig: ἀνταναπληρῶ τὰ ὑστερήματα τῶν θλίψεων τοῦ Χριστοῦ (antanaplērō ta hysterēmata tōn thlipseōn tou Christou)
r: Acts 9:4; 2 Corinthians 1:5; 2 Corinthians 4:10-12; Philippians 3:10; 1 Peter 4:13; Revelation 6:11

p: Oikonomia is the work of a household manager; God put Paul in charge of a trust.
b: Oikonomia was the job of a steward who ran a household for its owner, often a trusted slave. Ephesians 3:2 uses the same word for Paul's commission ('the task of managing God's grace for you'), and Ephesians 1:10 and 3:9 use it for God's own 'plan'. Here, as in Ephesians 3:2, the stress is on Paul's assignment. 'To bring God's word to its full extent' (plērōsai, 'to fill, complete') may mean to preach it fully, or to carry it to the Gentiles and so complete its course (Romans 15:19).
orig: τὴν οἰκονομίαν τοῦ θεοῦ (tēn oikonomian tou theou)

p: In Paul a mystery is God's plan once hidden and now made known, not a riddle.
b: Mystērion in Greek religion meant secret rites revealed only to initiates. In Daniel 2 (Aramaic raz) and in the Dead Sea Scrolls it is God's hidden plan that he reveals. Paul's use is the second: a secret God kept 'from the ages and from the generations' and has now shown openly 'to his saints', not to a select few. Romans 16:25-26 speaks of 'the mystery kept in silence for long ages, but now brought into the open', and Ephesians 3:5-6 says the mystery is that the Gentiles are heirs together.
orig: τὸ μυστήριον (to mystērion)

a: Christ in you, the hope of glory
t: Christ in you, or Christ among you?
p: En hymin can mean 'in you' (inside each one) or 'among you' (Gentiles).
b: Christos en hymin: 'Christ in you'. Because the verse has just said 'among the Gentiles', many read 'Christ among you Gentiles': the mystery is that the Messiah of Israel is now present among the nations (Ephesians 3:6). Others read 'in you' as Christ living within each believer (Galatians 2:20; Romans 8:10). The Greek allows both, and Paul may mean both. 'The hope of glory' points ahead to 3:4, 'you too will be revealed with him in glory'.
orig: Χριστὸς ἐν ὑμῖν (Christos en hymin)

p: Panta anthropon is repeated three times, perhaps against a teaching for the few.
b: Paul says 'every person' (panta anthrōpon) three times in one verse. If the teachers at Colossae offered a higher wisdom for those who had seen visions (2:18), the repetition answers that Christ's wisdom is for everyone. Teleios, 'complete', was also a word for the fully initiated in the mystery religions, and Paul gives it to every believer 'in Christ'.
orig: πάντα ἄνθρωπον (panta anthrōpon)

p: Energeia and energeo: the source of the English 'energy'.
b: Paul's own toil and struggle (kopiō, agōnizomai, an athlete's word) are driven by 'his working which is at work in me' (tēn energeian autou tēn energoumenēn). The same word for God's working comes in 2:12: faith in God's working raised the believers with Christ. The struggle continues in 2:1 ('what a hard fight', agōn) and in Epaphras' prayers (4:12).
orig: κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν αὐτοῦ (kata tēn energeian autou)

p: The leading city of the Lycus valley, about 12 miles (19 km) west of Colossae.
b: Lightfoot puts Colossae 'some twelve miles east of Laodicea' (about 19 km). Tacitus says that in the year of Nero's fourth consulship (AD 60) Laodicea was overthrown by an earthquake and rebuilt from its own resources, without help from Rome (Annals 14.27). He does not name Colossae. Eusebius' Chronicle, as Lightfoot reports it, puts the quake a few years later and includes Hierapolis and Colossae. The letter does not mention any earthquake. Laodicea's church receives the letter of Revelation 3:14-22.

a: never seen my face in person
p: Paul writes to believers who knew him only by name, through Epaphras.
b: Literally 'have not seen my face in the flesh'. This verse, with 1:4, 7-9, shows that Paul had not founded the church and had not been there. Acts never mentions Colossae. Paul's authority over a church he had not visited rests on his commission to the Gentiles (1:25) and on his tie to their founder, Epaphras. The same situation lies behind Romans (Romans 1:10-13).

a: all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge
p: Wisdom as hidden treasure is an image from Proverbs and Isaiah.
b: Proverbs tells the reader to search for wisdom 'as you would buried treasure' (Proverbs 2:4), and Isaiah 45:3 speaks of 'treasures kept in the dark'. Jewish writers spoke of Wisdom hidden with God. Colossians says these treasures are 'hidden' in Christ: not out of reach, but stored where believers already are. If the teachers at Colossae offered secret knowledge, this verse says there is nowhere else to look. Compare Romans 11:33.

p: Pithanologia: speech that is merely persuasive, the art of a clever speaker.
b: Pithanologia means plausible speech, argument that convinces by its polish rather than its truth. Paul makes the same contrast about his own preaching in 1 Corinthians 2:4: 'not in persuasive wisdom, but in the proof of the Spirit and of power'.
orig: πιθανολογίᾳ (pithanologia)

t: Good order and a solid front
p: Taxis and stereoma can be military words: ranks in order, a firm line.
b: Taxis is 'order' and can mean soldiers drawn up in ranks; stereōma is 'firmness'. Lightfoot read both as a military picture, 'your orderly array' and 'solid front, close phalanx', and pointed to 1 Maccabees 9:14, where stereōma is the strong wing of an army: Paul, absent in body, looks on in spirit and sees the Colossians' ranks unbroken. Others take the words in a plain sense, 'your orderliness and the firmness of your faith'. The Plain English Translation keeps 'standing' twice so either picture can be seen.
orig: τὴν τάξιν καὶ τὸ στερέωμα (tēn taxin kai to sterēoma)

a: you received Christ Jesus, the Lord
p: Paralambano is the word for receiving teaching handed down, like a rabbi's tradition.
b: Paralambanō, 'receive', with its partner paradidōmi, 'hand on', is the language of tradition, used by Jewish teachers and by Paul: 'I handed on to you ... what I also received' (1 Corinthians 15:3; 11:23). What the Colossians received was not only teaching about Christ but 'Christ Jesus, the Lord' himself. Two verses later Paul warns against 'human tradition' (paradosis): one tradition is set against another.
orig: παρελάβετε τὸν Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν τὸν κύριον (parelabete ton Christon Iēsoun ton kyrion)

a: Be rooted in him and keep being built up in him
p: Two pictures mixed: a tree with roots, a house rising on a foundation.
b: 'Rooted' is a perfect participle (rooted once, and staying so), while 'built up' is present (still going up). The mix of a planted tree and a building comes also in Ephesians 3:17 ('rooted and founded in love') and 1 Corinthians 3:9. It picks up 1:23, 'with your foundation laid and standing firm'.

p: Sylagogeo is a rare word: to carry off as booty, to kidnap.
b: Sylagōgeō appears only here in the New Testament. It means to lead away as plunder, as soldiers drove off captives and loot. The readers had been 'rescued' and 'moved' into the Son's kingdom (1:13); the false teaching would carry them off again into captivity.
orig: συλαγωγῶν (sylagōgōn)

p: Only here does the New Testament use philosophia. Scholars have proposed many identities for it.
b: The letter never names its opponents, so the teaching must be pieced together: 'philosophy' and 'human tradition' (2:8), 'the basic elements of the world' (2:8, 20), circumcision (2:11), food, festivals, new moons and Sabbaths (2:16), self-humbling and 'the worship of angels' and visions (2:18), and rules about not touching or tasting (2:21-23). Proposals include: a Jewish mysticism of fasting and heavenly ascent (Fred Francis); Essene-like Judaism mixed with speculation (J. B. Lightfoot, 1875); a syncretism of Phrygian folk belief, local Judaism and Christianity (Clinton Arnold); Epicurean philosophy (Norman DeWitt, St Paul and Epicurus, 1954); or no definite group of false teachers, only encouragement for a young church (Morna Hooker, 'Were There False Teachers in Colossae?', 1973). Jewish writers such as Philo and Josephus called the Jewish way of life a 'philosophy'.
orig: φιλοσοφίας (philosophias)

a: the basic elements of the world
t: The basic elements of the world
p: Ta stoicheia tou kosmou: the ABCs, the four elements, or the spirits linked with them?
b: Galatians 4:3 uses the same phrase: 'we were kept in slavery under the basic elements of the world'. Stoicheia meant things in a row: the letters of the alphabet, the first principles of a subject, the physical elements (earth, water, air, fire), the stars, and in later texts the spirits thought to rule them. Here the elements are paired with 'human tradition' and with rules about food and days (2:20-21). The readings are listed on the topic page. The Plain English Translation uses the site's fixed wording from Galatians.
orig: τὰ στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου (ta stoicheia tou kosmou)

a: all the fullness of deity makes its home bodily
t: The whole fullness of deity, bodily
p: Theotes means the being of God itself; somatikos may mean 'in a body' or 'in reality'.
b: Theotēs is 'deity', the quality of being God; it differs from theiotēs, 'divine nature' as seen in creation (Romans 1:20). The present tense 'makes its home' says this is still so of the risen Christ. Sōmatikōs, 'bodily', has been read as: in a human body (the incarnation, John 1:14); in reality, as against the 'shadow' of 2:17; or as a whole, organically, the fullness gathered in one body. Christian teachers from the 300s onward cited this verse against the idea that Christ was a lesser divine being.
orig: πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος σωματικῶς (pan to plērōma tēs theotētos sōmatikōs)

p: A play on words: in him is the fullness, and in him you have been filled.
b: Plērōma ('fullness', 2:9) and peplērōmenoi ('made full', 2:10) share a root. Whatever the teachers offered as a way to fullness, Paul says the readers already have it in Christ, who is head over every power they might fear.
orig: ἐστὲ ἐν αὐτῷ πεπληρωμένοι (este en autō peplērōmenoi)

a: circumcision, one not done by human hands
p: Moses and Jeremiah already spoke of circumcising the heart.
b: Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:11). The Torah itself looks for an inner circumcision: 'So circumcise the foreskin of your heart' (Deuteronomy 10:16), and 'The LORD your God will circumcise your heart' (Deuteronomy 30:6; compare Jeremiah 4:4). 'Not done by human hands' (acheiropoiētos) is used in the New Testament for what God makes rather than people (Mark 14:58; 2 Corinthians 5:1). The teachers at Colossae may have urged circumcision (compare Galatians); Paul says the readers have already received the real thing.
orig: περιτομῇ ἀχειροποιήτῳ (peritomē acheiropoiētō)
r: Genesis 17:11; Deuteronomy 10:16; Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4; Romans 2:28-29; Philippians 3:3; Mark 14:58

p: 'The circumcision of Christ' may be the circumcision Christ gives, or Christ's own death.
b: Readings: (1) the circumcision Christ performs on believers, which is baptism or the new birth (Christ as the one who circumcises); (2) the circumcision that Christ himself underwent, meaning his death, when 'the body of the flesh' was stripped off at the cross (some read 1:22 this way); (3) circumcision that belongs to Christ, Christian as against Jewish. The stripping off 'of the body of the flesh' is then either the believer's old self (3:9) or Christ's body in death. The Catholic Catechism calls baptism 'that "circumcision of Christ"' (527).

a: In baptism you were buried with him
p: Romans 6 makes the same move, with one difference: there the rising is still ahead.
b: Romans 6:4 says, 'By baptism into death, then, we were buried with him', and goes on 'we will certainly be part of his resurrection too' (Romans 6:5), a future. Colossians says the readers have already been raised with Christ (also 3:1). Many critical scholars count this 'already raised' among the signs of a later hand; others note that Paul too speaks of new life now (Romans 6:11; Galatians 2:20), and Colossians still looks ahead to glory (3:4). The editions differ on the form of the word: NA28, SBLGNT and Tregelles read baptismos, the Tyndale House edition, Westcott-Hort and the Byzantine text baptisma. Both mean 'baptism'.
orig: συνταφέντες αὐτῷ ἐν τῷ βαπτισμῷ (syntaphentes autō en tō baptismō)

t: Raised in baptism, or in him?
p: En hō can mean 'in it' (baptism) or 'in whom' (Christ). The Plain English Translation chooses one; the other is just as possible.
b: The Greek en hō, 'in which' or 'in whom', is the same phrase that opens 2:11, where it means 'in him', Christ. Here it can point back to baptism, the nearest word ('in it you were also raised'), or to Christ, as in 2:11 ('in him you were also raised'). The Plain English Translation follows the nearer word, but either reading fits the passage: believers are raised with Christ, and baptism is where that union is marked. The choice bears on the baptism card on this chapter, since one reading ties the rising more closely to the rite and the other to Christ himself, 'through faith in God's working'.
orig: ἐν ᾧ καὶ συνηγέρθητε (en hō kai synēgerthēte)

p: The Greek can mean faith that trusts God's power, or a faith that God's power produces.
b: Dia tēs pisteōs tēs energeias tou theou: most read 'faith in God's working' (objective), faith that trusts the power that raised Jesus. A few read 'the faith that God's working produces'.
orig: διὰ τῆς πίστεως τῆς ἐνεργείας τοῦ θεοῦ (dia tēs pisteōs tēs energeias tou theou)

a: God gave you life together with him
p: Ephesians 2:1, 5 says the same; the Plain English Translation uses its wording.
b: 'You were dead, in your trespasses and your sins' (Ephesians 2:1), and 'he gave us life together with Christ' (Ephesians 2:5). The Greek verb syzōopoieō is the same in both. Colossians adds 'the uncircumcision of your flesh': the readers were Gentiles, outside the covenant sign, and dead in more than one sense. The subject is unnamed in the Greek; the Plain English Translation supplies 'God' from the end of 2:12. The switch from 'you' to 'us' in 'He forgave us' puts Paul, a Jew, among the forgiven.

t: The IOU nailed to the cross
p: Cheirographon was a handwritten note of debt signed by the debtor.
b: A cheirographon was a document written or signed in the debtor's own hand, an IOU. Papyri from Egypt show many. The image is that God canceled it: 'wiped away' (as ink was washed off papyrus) and 'nailed to the cross', as the charge against a crucified man was posted above him (Mark 15:26). Readings of what the bill is: the debt of sin written against humanity, signed as it were by each person's own failures; or the law of Moses with its decrees, which condemned (compare Ephesians 2:15, 'the law of commandments with its rules').
orig: χειρόγραφον τοῖς δόγμασιν (cheirographon tois dogmasin)

a: He stripped the rulers and the authorities bare
p: Apekdysamenos is a middle verb, which may mean 'stripped off from himself'.
b: Apekdysamenos is middle in form, 'having stripped off from himself'. Lightfoot traced three readings: the Latin fathers (Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine) took it as Christ 'putting off his flesh'; the Greek fathers (Chrysostom, Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret) as Christ stripping off and casting away the powers that had clung to him; and Jerome's Latin exspolians, 'despoiling', gave the common reading, 'having disarmed the rulers and authorities', which the Plain English Translation follows. The same root appears in 2:11 ('the stripping off of the body of the flesh') and 3:9 ('you have taken off the old self'). On the common reading, the defeated powers are stripped of weapons and rank, as captives were before a Roman triumph.
orig: ἀπεκδυσάμενος (apekdysamenos)

a: leading them in his victory parade by it
p: Thriambeuo: to lead captives in a victory parade through the city.
b: In a Roman triumph, the victorious general rode through Rome with his captured enemies and spoils on show, and the captive leaders were often killed afterward. Paul uses the same verb in 2 Corinthians 2:14: 'who always leads us in his victory parade in Christ'. The site keeps 'victory parade' in both places. Here the defeated powers are the captives. 'By it' (en autō) may mean the cross (2:14) or 'in him', Christ; if God is the subject through the passage, Christ is meant.
orig: θριαμβεύσας αὐτοὺς ἐν αὐτῷ (thriambeusas autous en autō)

a: a festival, a new moon or Sabbaths
p: The three are the standard list of Israel's sacred times, from yearly to monthly to weekly.
b: The Hebrew Bible lists them together: 'for the Sabbaths, the New Moons and the set feasts' (1 Chronicles 23:31), 'her festivals, her new moons, her sabbaths' (Hosea 2:11), and Ezekiel 45:17. So the teaching at Colossae involved the Jewish calendar, at least in part. Paul does not condemn the days; he forbids anyone to 'sit in judgment' over the readers about them, as Romans 14:5 leaves the choice to each person: 'Each one should be fully sure in their own mind.' See the card on this chapter.

p: The Torah has food laws but few rules about drink; the concern may have been fasting.
b: Brōsis and posis are acts, 'eating' and 'drinking'. The SBL and Tyndale House editions join them with 'or', as the rest of the verse does; NA28 has 'and' (see the variant). The law of Moses forbids some foods, but says little about drink beyond the Nazirite vow and priests on duty (Numbers 6:3; Leviticus 10:9). Since 2:18 and 2:23 speak of self-humbling and harsh treatment of the body, many think the teachers urged fasting and abstinence, perhaps to prepare for visions, as some Jewish visionaries fasted before revelations (Daniel 10:2-3).
orig: ἐν βρώσει ἢ ἐν πόσει (en brōsei ē en posei)

p: The shadow is cast by the body; the real thing belongs to Christ.
b: Skia, 'shadow', and sōma, 'body', were a Greek pair for appearance and reality. Hebrews uses the same picture of the law as 'a shadow of the good things to come' (Hebrews 10:1; 8:5). 'Of what is to come' looks from the time the laws were given toward Christ. 'Body' here also hints at Christ's body, the church (1:18; 2:19). On whether the shadow means the end of the Sabbath for Christians, the churches differ (see the card).
orig: ἅ ἐστιν σκιὰ τῶν μελλόντων, τὸ δὲ σῶμα τοῦ Χριστοῦ (ha estin skia tōn mellontōn, to de sōma tou Christou)

a: act as umpire and rule you out
p: Katabrabeuo: to rule against someone, as a judge in the games disqualifies a runner.
b: A brabeus was the umpire at the games who gave out the prize (brabeion, Philippians 3:14). Katabrabeuō means to rule against, to disqualify. The same root returns in 3:15, 'Let the peace of Christ be the umpire in your hearts': not the visionary teacher but Christ's peace is to decide.
orig: καταβραβευέτω (katabrabeuetō)

p: Tapeinophrosyne here is probably fasting and other practices of self-denial.
b: Tapeinophrosynē is the 'humility' Paul praises in 3:12. Here it goes with 'the worship of angels' and with rules about food, and in Jewish writing the Hebrew idea behind it, 'to humble the soul', means to fast (Leviticus 16:29; Psalm 35:13). So the teachers probably required fasting and other self-denial. 'Delights in' (thelōn en) follows a Septuagint way of saying 'takes pleasure in'; Lightfoot took it as 'taking delight in, devoting himself to'.
orig: θέλων ἐν ταπεινοφροσύνῃ (thelōn en tapeinophrosynē)

t: Worshiping angels, or worship with the angels?
p: The Greek can mean worship given to angels, or the worship angels offer, which a visionary joins.
b: Thrēskeia tōn angelōn can be objective, 'worship directed to angels', or subjective, 'the angels' worship'. Objective: the teachers prayed to or called on angels. Lightfoot quotes Theodoret, who says this 'disease' long remained in Phrygia, and canon 35 of a later church council at Laodicea, which forbids Christians to 'invoke angels'; Clinton Arnold links it to the invocation of angels in local magic. Subjective: Fred Francis argued that the teachers sought, through fasting, to enter heaven in vision and join the angels' worship before God's throne, a hope seen in the Dead Sea Scrolls' Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice. Either way, Paul's reply is that Christ is head over all such powers (2:10).
orig: θρησκείᾳ τῶν ἀγγέλων (thrēskeia tōn angelōn)

a: entering into the things he has seen
p: Embateuo is a puzzle: 'entering', or 'busying himself with' his visions.
b: Ha heoraken embateuōn is one of the hardest phrases in Paul. Embateuō means 'step into, enter, take possession'. Lightfoot notes that the phrase is usually explained as 'parading' or 'poring over his visions', and that the verb can mean 'busying himself with' a subject (2 Maccabees 2:30 uses it of a historian going into every detail). Read the plain way, the visionary 'enters' the heavenly places he claims to have seen. Lightfoot found the phrase so hard that he suspected an early copying error, and conjectured kenembateuōn, 'treading on air'. The Byzantine text adds 'not' (see the variant).
orig: ἃ ἑόρακεν ἐμβατεύων (ha heoraken embateuōn)

a: held firm by its joints and ligaments
p: Ephesians 4:16 says the same in nearly the same words; the Plain English Translation follows it where the Greek matches.
b: Ephesians 4:16: 'From him the whole body is fitted together and held firm by every joint that supplies it'. Both letters picture the head as the source of the body's supply and growth. The visionary who has lost his hold on the head is like a limb cut off from what keeps it alive.
orig: διὰ τῶν ἁφῶν καὶ συνδέσμων (dia tōn haphōn kai syndesmōn)

a: Do not take hold! Do not taste! Do not even touch!
p: Paul seems to quote the teachers' own rules, with mockery in the repetition.
b: The three commands sound like slogans, and most translations put them in quotation marks. They go from stronger to weaker, 'take hold', 'taste', 'even touch', to show how small the rules had become. They may concern food and drink (2:16), or ritual purity more widely. 1 Timothy 4:3 also warns against teachers who 'stop people from marrying and tell them to keep clear of foods'.

a: the commandments and teachings of people
p: The phrase echoes Isaiah 29:13 in the Greek, as Jesus quotes it in Mark 7:7.
b: Isaiah complains that the people's fear of God 'is a command made by humans and learned by heart' (Isaiah 29:13). The Septuagint has 'teaching human commandments and teachings', and Jesus quotes that form against the tradition of washing in Mark 7:7. Colossians uses the same words, entalmata kai didaskalias tōn anthrōpōn, so rules about touching and tasting are set in the line of the traditions Jesus criticized.
orig: τὰ ἐντάλματα καὶ διδασκαλίας τῶν ἀνθρώπων (ta entalmata kai didaskalias tōn anthrōpōn)

p: Ethelothreskia: a word made up for the occasion, 'worship by one's own will'.
b: Ethelothrēskia appears nowhere before this verse. It joins thelō ('wish', as in 2:18) to thrēskeia ('worship', as in 'the worship of angels'), and means worship people invent and choose for themselves. With 'self-humbling' and 'not sparing the body' (apheidia sōmatos, severe treatment), it describes an ascetic piety that looked wise.
orig: ἐθελοθρησκίᾳ (ethelothrēskia)

a: against the flesh's craving to be filled
p: The last clause of chapter 2 can be read in opposite ways.
b: Ouk en timē tini pros plēsmonēn tēs sarkos is literally 'not in any honor, toward the filling of the flesh'. Most translations read 'of no value against the indulgence of the flesh' (the rules look wise but do not curb desire), as the Plain English Translation does. Others read 'not of any honor, but serving only to satisfy the flesh' (the rules feed the flesh's pride), or take 'honor' in the sense of proper respect owed to the body. Plēsmonē means being filled, satisfied, glutted.
orig: οὐκ ἐν τιμῇ τινι πρὸς πλησμονὴν τῆς σαρκός (ouk en timē tini pros plēsmonēn tēs sarkos)

p: The most quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament stands behind this line.
b: 'Sit at my right hand' (Psalm 110:1) is applied to the risen Jesus throughout the New Testament (Mark 12:36; Acts 2:34-35; Ephesians 1:20; Hebrews 1:13). The right hand is the place of honor and power. Since the believers 'were raised with Christ', their concerns are to be where he is. The verse answers the visionaries who sought heaven by ascent (2:18): believers are already joined to the one at God's right hand.

a: your life is kept hidden away with Christ in God
p: Believers have died and been raised, yet their life is hidden until Christ appears.
b: Colossians has a strong 'already': died with Christ (2:20; 3:3), buried and raised (2:12), seated where he is (3:1). It also has a 'not yet': the life is 'hidden' and will be 'revealed' only when Christ is (3:4). Readers who see a later author point to the strong 'already'; others say the balance is the same as in Romans 6 and Philippians 3:20-21.

p: Phaneroo: made visible. The coming of Christ is pictured as an unveiling.
b: Colossians does not use parousia, 'coming', the word of 1 Thessalonians 4:15. It speaks of Christ being 'revealed' (phanerōthē), made visible, and the believers 'revealed with him in glory'. The same verb was used of the mystery 'made plain to his saints' (1:26). What is hidden now (3:3) will be seen.
orig: ὅταν ὁ Χριστὸς φανερωθῇ (hotan ho Christos phanerōthē)

a: the parts of you that belong to the earth
t: Put to death your earthly parts
p: Literally 'the members (body parts) on the earth': a vivid picture, then a list of sins.
b: Ta melē ta epi tēs gēs is literally 'the limbs that are on the earth'. Paul names body parts and then lists sins, as if the sins were limbs to be cut off (compare Matthew 5:29-30; Romans 6:13). 'On the earth' answers 'what is above' in 3:1-2. The list matches Ephesians 5:3, 5: 'sexual immorality and any kind of impurity or greed'.
orig: νεκρώσατε οὖν τὰ μέλη τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς (nekrōsate oun ta melē ta epi tēs gēs)

p: Pleonexia, wanting more, is called the worship of a false god.
b: Pleonexia is wanting more than one's share. Ephesians 5:5 also links the greedy person with idolatry. Jewish teachers made a similar link: the Ten Words begin with 'no other gods' and end with 'do not covet'. Jesus says no one can serve God and money (Matthew 6:24). Here the list of sins of desire ends with the one that sounds most respectable, and calls it the worst.
orig: τὴν πλεονεξίαν, ἥτις ἐστὶν εἰδωλολατρία (tēn pleonexian, hētis estin eidōlolatria)

p: Orge, often rendered 'wrath': God's settled opposition to evil, coming at the judgment.
b: This site renders orgē 'anger' (gloss 'wrath'), as in Romans. 'Comes' is present tense, but it may describe what is sure to come (Romans 2:5; 1 Thessalonians 1:10). The Plain English Translation matches Ephesians 5:6, which has the same Greek. Some old manuscripts lack 'on the people who disobey' (see the variant).
orig: ἡ ὀργὴ τοῦ θεοῦ (hē orgē tou theou)

p: Clothing language runs through 3:8-14, perhaps from the practice of baptism.
b: 'Take them all off' (3:8), 'taken off the old self' (3:9), 'put on the new self' (3:10), 'put on ... compassion' (3:12), 'put on love' (3:14). Ephesians 4:22-24 uses the same pictures, and Galatians 3:27 says, 'Every one of you who was baptized into Christ has put Christ on'. Many scholars think the language comes from baptism, where the person going into the water took off old clothes and came up to put on new ones. 'Self' translates anthrōpos, 'human being': the old humanity in Adam and the new in Christ.
orig: ἀπεκδυσάμενοι τὸν παλαιὸν ἄνθρωπον (apekdysamenoi ton palaion anthrōpon)

a: to match the image of the one who created it
p: The new self is made new to fit the image of God, the Genesis language of 1:15.
b: 'In God's image he created him' (Genesis 1:27). The new humanity is 'being made new' (present tense, an ongoing work) 'in knowledge', a pointed phrase in a letter about false knowledge, according to the image of its Creator. Since Christ is 'the image of the God who cannot be seen' (1:15), the renewal is a matter of being made like Christ, as Romans 8:29 says believers are 'formed to match the image of his Son'.

p: A barbarian was anyone who did not speak Greek; Scythians were the byword for the wildest of them.
b: Greeks called anyone who did not speak Greek a barbaros, imitating speech that sounded like 'bar-bar'. The Scythians, horse nomads north of the Black Sea, were the proverbial savages of Greek and Roman writing. Some suggest the list pairs opposites (Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian and Scythian, slave and free), with Scythians as the far end of the barbarians, or Scythians as a source of slaves. Galatians 3:28 has a shorter list: 'There is no Jew and no Greek. There is no slave and no free person. There is no male and female.' Colossians has no 'male and female'.
orig: βάρβαρος, Σκύθης, δοῦλος, ἐλεύθερος (barbaros, Skythēs, doulos, eleutheros)

a: Christ is all things and in all
t: Christ is all, and in all
p: Panta kai en pasin Christos: Christ is everything, and in everyone (or everything).
b: The Greek has no verb: '[the] all and in all, Christ'. Pasin may be masculine ('in all people') or neuter ('in all things'). The line takes up the 'all things' of the hymn (1:16-20) and applies it to the church: the distinctions that ranked people are not erased in daily life (3:18-4:1 still speaks to slaves and masters), but they no longer decide who belongs or who is worth more.
orig: τὰ πάντα καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν Χριστός (ta panta kai en pasin Christos)

a: God's chosen ones, holy and loved
t: Israel's titles given to the church
p: Chosen, holy and loved are the names of Israel in the Old Testament.
b: The three words were titles of Israel: 'a holy people', 'chosen' (Deuteronomy 7:6), loved by God (Deuteronomy 7:8). Paul gives them to Gentile believers, as 1 Peter 2:9 does. The J lens asks whether this means the church replaces Israel, joins Israel, or shares Israel's blessings; Romans 11 warns Gentile believers not to boast over the branches.

a: the tie that makes them complete
p: Syndesmos tes teleiotetos: love is the bond that holds all the other virtues together.
b: Syndesmos is a binding tie; the same word is used for the body's 'ligaments' in 2:19, and Ephesians 4:3 uses it for peace, 'the tie that binds you'. Love is pictured as the belt or outer garment that holds the rest of the clothing in place. Teleiotēs, 'completeness, maturity', echoes 'complete in Christ' (1:28). Some take the genitive as 'the bond that leads to perfection', others as 'the perfect bond'.
orig: σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος (syndesmos tēs teleiotētos)

a: be the umpire in your hearts
p: Brabeuo: to act as umpire, to decide. The same root as 2:18.
b: Most English versions say 'rule'. The verb brabeuō means to act as the umpire who decides. In 2:18 the visionary tried to 'rule you out' (katabrabeuō). Here the umpire is the peace of Christ, settling disputes between members of one body (3:13).
orig: βραβευέτω (brabeuetō)

a: psalms, hymns and songs from the Spirit
p: The same three words as Ephesians 5:19. Early church singing, and the churches' later debates about it.
b: Ephesians 5:19 has 'in psalms, hymns and songs from the Spirit', and the Plain English Translation uses the same words. 'Psalms' may mean the biblical Psalms; 'hymns' and 'songs' may be new Christian compositions such as the hymn in 1:15-20. Many scholars think the three overlap rather than name three kinds. The singing teaches and warns: it is a way of letting 'the word of Christ' live among them. Some churches in the Reformed tradition (exclusive psalmody) have sung only biblical psalms, reading all three words as names for psalms; most churches sing other hymns as well.

p: Only here does the New Testament say 'the word of Christ': his teaching, or the message about him.
b: Ho logos tou Christou may mean the message about Christ (the good news, 1:5) or Christ's own teaching. Some copyists changed it to 'the word of God' or 'the word of the Lord' (see the variant). 'Live in you' (enoikeitō) uses the 'home' language of 1:19 and 2:9: as the fullness makes its home in Christ, his word is to make its home in the church.
orig: ὁ λόγος τοῦ Χριστοῦ (ho logos tou Christou)

a: in the name of the Lord Jesus
p: To act 'in the name' of someone is to act as their representative, under their authority.
b: In the Old Testament, prophets speak and priests bless 'in the name of the LORD'. Here every word and deed is done 'in the name of the Lord Jesus', so the whole of ordinary life becomes service done as his. The closing thanks to God 'through him' echoes Ephesians 5:20: 'always giving thanks for everything to God the Father, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ'.

a: Wives, submit yourselves to your husbands
t: Wives and husbands: the household code
p: The same instruction as Ephesians 5:22-24, but shorter; how far it reaches is debated.
b: The household code (3:18-4:1) addresses three pairs of a household in turn: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters. Aristotle called these three pairs 'the primary and smallest parts of the household' (Politics 1.1253b). Christian readers differ: complementarians read a lasting order of male headship in marriage; egalitarians read a first-century arrangement, softened by 'in the Lord', that Ephesians 5:21 frames with mutual submission; others read it as advice that let the church live without scandal in its society. 'As is proper' translates anēken, which is past in form ('was proper'); most read it as 'is proper', and some see in the past form a hint at accepted custom. The Plain English Translation's 'submit yourselves' matches Ephesians 5:21, 'submitting yourselves'. The churches' teaching is set out on the 'Where Christians differ' card on Ephesians 5 (Ephesians 5:21-33), which this page does not repeat.
orig: ὑποτάσσεσθε τοῖς ἀνδράσιν ὡς ἀνῆκεν ἐν κυρίῳ (hypotassesthe tois andrasin hōs anēken en kyriō)

a: do not turn bitter against them
p: Pikraino: to become sour or harsh toward someone. A limit on the husband's power.
b: Mē pikrainesthe pros autas is 'do not be embittered toward them'. A Roman husband held legal and social power over his wife. The code tells husbands not only to love but not to turn sour and harsh.
orig: μὴ πικραίνεσθε πρὸς αὐτάς (mē pikrainesthe pros autas)

a: do not keep irritating your children
p: Erethizo: to stir up, nag, provoke. Roman fathers had near-total power over their children.
b: Roman law gave a father (paterfamilias) great power over his children, even adult ones. The code addresses children directly as members of the church (3:20) and then limits fathers: do not keep provoking them, 'so that they do not lose heart' (athymeō, become discouraged, lose spirit). Ephesians 6:4 uses a different verb, 'do not stir your children to anger'.
orig: μὴ ἐρεθίζετε τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν (mē erethizete ta tekna hymōn)

a: Slaves, obey your human masters in everything
p: The longest part of the code speaks to slaves. It does not condemn slavery; it was later used for and against it.
b: Four verses go to slaves and one to masters. The slaves are addressed as full members who hear the letter and answer to the Lord. Readers of Philemon note that Onesimus, a slave from Colossae, travels with this letter (4:9). The code does not say slavery is wrong, and for centuries it was quoted by defenders of slavery; enslaved Christians and abolitionists read in it that masters have 'a Lord in heaven' (4:1) and that God shows 'no favoritism' (3:25). The Plain English Translation matches Ephesians 6:5-6 where the Greek matches. The churches' views are set out on the 'Where Christians differ' cards on Ephesians 6 (Ephesians 6:5-9) and on Philemon (Philemon 15-16), which this page does not repeat.

p: Under Roman law a slave could not inherit; here slaves are promised the inheritance.
b: Tēn antapodosin tēs klēronomias is 'the repayment that is the inheritance'. A slave could own little and inherit nothing. The promise turns this around: slaves are heirs, like the 'lot of the saints' in 1:12. 'The Lord Christ is the one you serve as slaves' can also be read as a command, 'Serve the Lord Christ!' (the verb form is the same); the Byzantine text adds 'for', which makes it a statement.
orig: τὴν ἀνταπόδοσιν τῆς κληρονομίας (tēn antapodosin tēs klēronomias)

p: Prosopolempsia, 'receiving the face': judging by who someone is.
b: The Greek word comes from a Hebrew idiom, 'to lift up the face' of someone, meaning to favor them (Deuteronomy 10:17; Leviticus 19:15). Here it cuts both ways: the slave who does wrong will be repaid, and so will the master (Ephesians 6:9, 'with him there is no favoritism').
orig: οὐκ ἔστιν προσωπολημψία (ouk estin prosōpolēmpsia)

a: what is just and what is equal
p: Isotes means 'equality' or 'fairness'; translators differ on how far it goes.
b: To dikaion kai tēn isotēta: 'what is just and equality'. Most translations take isotēs as 'fairness' (fair treatment). In Greek writers it often meant 'equality' (Paul uses it so in 2 Corinthians 8:13-14). Some readers think Paul asks masters to treat slaves as equals in the Lord. 'You too have a Lord in heaven' plays on kyrios, which means both 'master' and 'Lord'.
orig: τὸ δίκαιον καὶ τὴν ἰσότητα (to dikaion kai tēn isotēta)

p: Gregoreo, 'keep awake', is the word of Jesus in Gethsemane.
b: Jesus told the disciples, 'Stay awake and pray' (Mark 14:38) and to keep awake for the coming of the Son of Man (Mark 13:35-37). Prayer 'with thanksgiving' runs through the whole letter (1:3, 12; 2:7; 3:15-17).
orig: γρηγοροῦντες (grēgorountes)

a: open a door for the word
p: An open door is Paul's picture for a chance to preach.
b: Paul uses the same picture in 1 Corinthians 16:9 and 2 Corinthians 2:12 (Acts 14:27 speaks of 'a door to faith'). A prisoner asks not for the prison door to open but for a door for the word. 'It is for this that I am bound' matches the wording of Ephesians 6:20, 'It is for this that I am an ambassador in a chain'.

p: The letter says Paul is a prisoner (4:3, 10, 18) but not where. Three cities are proposed.
b: Rome: Paul was held there for two years (Acts 28:16, 30); this is the traditional view, and the subscription in the Textus Receptus says 'written from Rome'. Caesarea: he was held there two years too (Acts 24:27). Ephesus: Acts does not record an imprisonment there, but Paul speaks of many imprisonments (2 Corinthians 11:23), and Ephesus is close to Colossae, which would make Onesimus' journey and Paul's request for a guest room (Philemon 22) easier. The question is the same for Philemon and Philippians.

p: Ton kairon exagorazomenoi: the same phrase as Ephesians 5:16.
b: 'Buying up the right moment' (Ephesians 5:16). Exagorazō is to buy up, as a merchant buys up all the goods in the market; kairos is a right moment, an opportunity, rather than clock time. 'Those outside' are the non-believing neighbors. The church is to make use of every chance to show and say the good news.
orig: τὸν καιρὸν ἐξαγοραζόμενοι (ton kairon exagorazomenoi)

a: have salt in them for flavor
p: Salt gave flavor and kept food from spoiling; Greek writers spoke of witty speech as salty.
b: In Greek usage, 'salt' could mean wit. Jesus says, 'Keep salt in yourselves' (Mark 9:50). Speech 'with grace' (en chariti) means attractive, kind speech, and perhaps also speech shaped by God's grace. Together they describe words that are pleasant, thoughtful and wise in answering outsiders.
orig: ἅλατι ἠρτυμένος (halati ērtymenos)

p: Colossians 4:7-8 and Ephesians 6:21-22 are almost word for word the same.
b: The longest exact match between the two letters is here: about thirty Greek words in a row. Ephesians 6:21 reads, 'Tychicus will make everything known to you. He is a beloved brother and a faithful servant in the Lord.' Colossians adds 'and a fellow slave'. The Plain English Translation follows Ephesians wherever the Greek matches. Those who think Paul wrote both see one man carrying both letters on one journey; those who think Ephesians was written later see a writer copying Colossians. Tychicus was from Asia (Acts 20:4).

p: Almost certainly the slave whose return Paul asks for in the letter to Philemon.
b: Onesimus ('useful') was a common slave name. He is 'one of you', from Colossae, and Philemon 10-16 asks his master to receive him back 'no longer as a slave' but as a brother. The same names appear in both letters (Archippus, Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, Luke), so most scholars think the two letters were sent together. Here Onesimus is introduced to the whole church as 'the faithful and beloved brother', with no word about his past.

p: A Macedonian from Thessalonica who traveled with Paul and shared his imprisonment.
b: Acts names Aristarchus among Paul's companions in the riot at Ephesus (Acts 19:29), on the journey to Jerusalem (Acts 20:4) and on the ship to Rome: 'Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us' (Acts 27:2). 'Fellow captive' (synaichmalōtos, literally 'fellow prisoner of war') may mean he shared Paul's prison, or chose to stay with him. In Philemon 24 he is a 'fellow worker', and Epaphras is the 'fellow captive' (Philemon 23).
orig: ὁ συναιχμάλωτός μου (ho synaichmalōtos mou)

p: John Mark, who left Paul and Barnabas in Pamphylia, is back at Paul's side.
b: John Mark had left Paul and Barnabas on their first journey (Acts 13:13), and Paul refused to take him again: 'Barnabas took Mark along and set sail for Cyprus' (Acts 15:39). Here he is with Paul, and the Colossians are told to welcome him. 2 Timothy 4:11 asks for him: 'he is of great use to me in the ministry'. Anepsios means 'cousin', not 'nephew' (the KJV's 'sister's son'). Papias, quoted by Eusebius, passes on the word of 'the presbyter' that 'Mark, having become the interpreter of Peter, wrote down accurately' what Peter remembered (Church History 3.39.15); tradition links this Mark with the Gospel of Mark.
orig: ὁ ἀνεψιὸς Βαρναβᾶ (ho anepsios Barnaba)
r: Acts 12:12, 25; Acts 13:13; Acts 15:37-39; 2 Timothy 4:11; Philemon 1:24; 1 Peter 5:13

p: Jesus (Yeshua, Joshua) was a common Jewish name; he also used the Latin name Justus.
b: 'Jesus' was the Greek form of Joshua, one of the most common Jewish names of the time. Many Jews also took a Greek or Latin name, as Saul was Paul and Joseph Barsabbas was Justus (Acts 1:23). This man appears only here.

a: the only ones from the circumcision
p: Of those with Paul, these few were Jewish believers. Which names the phrase covers is debated.
b: 'From the circumcision' means Jewish believers. Aristarchus, Mark and Jesus Justus are the three just named, but some think it covers only Mark and Justus. Luke (4:14) is then usually taken to be a Gentile, which is the main evidence that Luke was not Jewish; some scholars dispute this. Paul says these Jewish coworkers had been a comfort: his work for Gentiles had not cut him off from his own people.

a: fighting for you in his prayers
p: Agonizomai is an athlete's word: Epaphras contends for them in prayer.
b: The same word as Paul's own 'strain' (1:29) and 'hard fight' (2:1). Epaphras' prayer asks that the church 'stand complete and fully convinced' in God's will, the aim of the whole letter (1:9, 28). 'Fully convinced' (peplērophorēmenoi) is the reading of the critical editions; the Byzantine text has 'complete' (peplērōmenoi; see the variant).
orig: ἀγωνιζόμενος (agōnizomenos)

p: The third city of the Lycus valley, known for its hot springs, north of Laodicea.
b: Hierapolis ('holy city', modern Pamukkale) stood across the Lycus valley from Laodicea, famous for its hot springs and white mineral terraces. Epaphras' work covered all three towns. Polycrates of Ephesus, quoted by Eusebius, says that Philip, 'one of the twelve apostles, ... sleeps in Hierapolis' (Church History 3.31.3), and Eusebius calls Papias 'bishop of the parish of Hierapolis' (3.36.2).

p: The only place that says Luke was a doctor. Church tradition makes him the author of Luke and Acts.
b: Luke is named here, in Philemon 24 and in 2 Timothy 4:11 ('Luke is the only one with me'). About AD 180 Irenaeus wrote that 'Luke also, the companion of Paul, recorded in a book the Gospel preached by him' (Against Heresies 3.1.1), and the church came to name this Luke as the author of the Gospel of Luke and Acts. The 'we' passages of Acts (Acts 16:10-17; 20:5-21:18; 27:1-28:16) put the author with Paul on the voyage to Rome, which fits.
orig: Λουκᾶς ὁ ἰατρὸς ὁ ἀγαπητός (Loukas ho iatros ho agapētos)

p: Here a coworker with no word of praise; 2 Timothy says he later left.
b: Demas is greeted here and in Philemon 24 as a 'fellow worker'. Colossians gives him no description, unlike the others. 2 Timothy 4:10 says that Demas left Paul behind: 'He loved the present age, and he has gone off to Thessalonica.'

a: the church that meets in her house
p: A woman hosts a church in her house. Some manuscripts make her a man, Nymphas.
b: The early churches met in homes (Romans 16:5; 1 Corinthians 16:19; Philemon 2). A woman's name with 'her house' means a woman who owned or headed a household and hosted the believers, as Lydia did in Philippi (Acts 16:15, 40). The accent of Nymphan decides the gender, and early manuscripts had no accents; the pronoun ('her', 'his', 'their') varies in the manuscripts (see the variant). The critical editions read 'her'.
orig: Νύμφαν ... αὐτῆς (Nymphan ... autēs)

p: A letter of Paul's that the Laodiceans had, which the Colossians were to read. What was it?
b: Views: (1) a lost letter of Paul to Laodicea; (2) our Ephesians, sent as a circular letter to several churches and passing through Laodicea (Lightfoot; Ephesians lacks 'in Ephesus' in some old manuscripts, and Marcion called it 'to the Laodiceans', as Tertullian reports); (3) Philemon; (4) a letter written by the Laodiceans. A short Latin 'Epistle to the Laodiceans', made of phrases mainly from Philippians, was copied in many Latin Bibles from the 500s to the Reformation but is not by Paul (see the deep dive on this chapter's page). The verse also shows that Paul's letters were read aloud in church and passed between churches, the first step toward their collection.

p: A member of Philemon's house church with a task to finish.
b: Philemon 2 greets 'Archippus our fellow soldier' and the church in Philemon's house. Some think he was Philemon's son. His 'service' (diakonia) is not described: perhaps leading the church while Epaphras was away, or perhaps (one theory) the task of persuading Philemon about Onesimus. That the message is given publicly suggests some concern.
orig: Ἀρχίππῳ (Archippō)

a: The greeting is in my own hand, Paul's
p: Paul dictated his letters and wrote the last greeting himself. The words match 1 Corinthians 16:21.
b: Letters were usually written by a scribe. The closing in the sender's own hand served as a signature and a mark of authenticity: 'The greeting is in my own hand, Paul's' (1 Corinthians 16:21); compare 2 Thessalonians 3:17 and Galatians 6:11. Those who think Colossians was written after Paul's death see this line as part of the letter's claim to be his; those who think he wrote it, perhaps with Timothy's help, see Paul taking the pen at the end, with chains on his wrists.

p: A last request: pray for the prisoner and honor his suffering.
b: Mnēmoneuete mou tōn desmōn. 'Remember' in the Bible often means to act on what one remembers: to pray, to help (Hebrews 13:3). The chains also add weight to the letter's teaching: the one who wrote it is suffering for it (1:24; 4:3).
orig: μνημονεύετέ μου τῶν δεσμῶν (mnēmoneuete mou tōn desmōn)
